status_reason: Material, location and target (protein and fat) are stated, so a first assessment is possible, but concentration ranges and flow conditions are missing, which decides path length and probe choice.
answer: Test NIR transmission or transflection on the clear whey stream and NIR diffuse reflection on the opaque concentrate, each calibrated against independent laboratory protein and fat results. A single shared interface is only a hypothesis; a transflection probe may serve both streams, which the comparison should test. The sources state that transmission fails when milk is too thick or fat-rich, so it should not be the concentrate method.

inline.headline: Test NIR transmission/transflection on whey and NIR diffuse reflection on concentrate in a paired laboratory comparison
inline.probe: Transmission/transflection probe with controlled path length (1-10 mm) for whey; flush-mounted diffuse reflection probe for concentrate
inline.install: Pilot sample loop or bypass on each stream; reflection probe flush-mounted in the pipe or vat for the concentrate
inline.test_against: One transflection probe used on both streams
inline.not_final_because: The sources give no dairy accuracy data; the NIR method range (780-2500 nm) exceeds the silica fiber limit of 2400 nm; the single-interface and per-stream calibration questions are open.

problems.text: The whey and the concentrate are two optical regimes: clear whey suits transmission or transflection, opaque concentrate suits reflection. Plan a separate interface decision and calibration for each stream; one shared interface is only a hypothesis to test.
Transmission cannot be used on the opaque, thick, fat-rich concentrate because the light cannot penetrate the sample.
Reflection is less representative for clear liquids and is sensitive to surface characteristics and fat globule size, so it is not a default choice for the whey.
The NIR range (780-2500 nm) is wider than the silica Vis-NIR fiber range (350-2400 nm); check spectrometer and fiber coverage above 2400 nm or confirm the bands used stay within the fiber range.

methods.why: Preferred for transparent or semi-transparent liquids such as whey; path length (usually 1-10 mm) must be controlled.
Used for opaque or concentrated dairy products such as the concentrate; probe flush-mounted in the pipe or vat.
Can add molecular specificity that NIR might miss, but MIR is limited to very thin layers (usually under 50 µm) and needs ATR attachments.
Gives information complementary to MIR, but needs special probes and weak signals can be masked by fluorescence.

experiment.objective: Decide, for each stream, which NIR interface and calibration predicts fat and protein best against independent laboratory results.
steps: Collect paired whey and concentrate samples across the production range, each with an independent laboratory protein and fat analysis (not the instrument's own calibration).
Measure whey with a transmission/transflection probe at a controlled path length (1-10 mm), and the concentrate with a flush-mounted reflection probe.
Measure both streams with one transflection probe to test whether a shared interface works.
Apply MSC/SNV scatter correction before PLS for fat and protein, and build a separate model per stream.
Validate on held-out samples, compare each interface's error with the laboratory values, and keep the best option per stream.
experiment.go_no_go: Accuracy criteria for fat and protein to be set by the client.

pathway.key_features: Not yet identified; fat and protein bands must be found by multivariate analysis of the lab spectra.
pathway.path_reason: A laboratory comparison of interfaces is needed before choosing an installation.

multispectral.why: Dairy sources name fluorescence, Raman and MIR ATR as possible additions for molecular specificity, but give no dairy result for a combination; a combination must first beat the best single NIR method.
multispectral.test: Only if single-method NIR models miss the target: measure the same concentrate spot with MIR ATR and NIR, and require the fused model to beat the best single NIR model on the same validation samples.

assumptions: The whey is clear enough for transmission or transflection; to be checked in the pilot.
The concentrate stays opaque across its operating range.
Laboratory protein and fat results are available for paired samples.
Protein and fat are the only target variables for the pilot.
